**1000 SCFM of natural gas is about 1607 Nm³/h.** This assumes US gas-industry standard conditions (60 °F, 14.696 psia) and normal conditions of 0 °C and 1.01325 bar (101.325 kPa, DIN 1343).

Method (calculated with Python, not taken from a table):
- 1000 ft³/min × 60 min/h × 0.0283168 m³/ft³ = 1699.0 m³/h at 60 °F, 14.696 psia
- To get to 0 °C at the same pressure, multiply by 273.15 / 288.706 = 0.94612, which gives **1607.5 Nm³/h**

The answer depends on which "standard" the SCFM figure uses:

| SCFM basis | Nm³/h (0 °C, 1.01325 bar) |
|---|---|
| 60 °F, 14.696 psia | 1607.5 |
| 60 °F, 14.73 psia (AGA gas-contract basis) | 1611.2 |
| 68 °F, 14.696 psia | 1583.1 |
| 70 °F, 14.7 psia | 1577.6 |

Some sources define Nm³ at 20 °C instead of 0 °C. On that basis the 60 °F result becomes about 1725 m³/h; this value was worked out by hand, not run.

I assumed ideal-gas scaling. The slight difference in natural gas compressibility (Z) between 60 °F and 0 °C was not included; I expect it to change the result by about 0.1% or less, but I did not calculate it.
